title: TS stream gateway: convergence scenarios for async-iterator / Web Streams interop
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Investigate and implement a small 'stream gateway' layer in the TypeScript SDK that normalizes and resolves edge cases between AsyncIterator-based streaming and WHATWG ReadableStream (Web Streams) consumers across Node/Deno/browser runtimes. Focus areas: cancellation propagation, backpressure harmony, resumable partial-streams after transient network errors, multi-consumer fanout, and minimizing bundle surface while retaining ergonomic APIs for application developers.
acceptance_criteria: Expose two ergonomic surface APIs: toAsyncIterator() and toWebStream() on streaming responses
Cancellation initiated from either API must reliably propagate to the underlying HTTP connection and runtime-agnostic cancel token
Backpressure from Web Streams .writer / reader must not cause unbounded memory growth in the SDK (bench tests below)
Provide a documented helper for safe fanout cloning of both async iterators and ReadableStreams
Add automated tests that simulate network hiccups and validate resumable semantics up to a token-offset boundary
Ship examples in the repo playground demonstrating Node (stream.Readable), browser ReadableStream, and async generator consumption patterns
No regressions on existing streaming integration tests (current baseline on CI: streaming-e2e v2025-02-04)
tasks: Design gateway API shape and TypeScript typings (include cancellation token type)
Prototype runtime adapters: Node Readable -> AsyncIterator, ReadableStream -> AsyncIterator, AsyncIterator -> ReadableStream
Implement cancellation plumbing with unified CancelController (cross-runtime) and hook into fetch/XHR/websocket adapters
Implement bounded buffering strategy and configurable watermarks to avoid OOM under slow consumers
Create fanout cloning helpers and document trade-offs (memory vs copy-vs-share semantics)
Add unit + integration tests, and a small perf harness to measure memory/latency under backpressure
Author examples and playground notebook in /examples/ts/stream-gateway
Write migration notes for existing SDK consumers (deprecate old stream helpers if applicable)
Code review and iterate on PR feedback
decisions: Use an internal lightweight CancelController (inspired by AbortController) to unify cancellation across AsyncIterator and Web Streams rather than relying on AbortSignal in all runtimes due to inconsistent support in older Node versions
Adopt a fixed-size ring buffer with high/low watermarks for cross-adapter buffering; watermark defaults tuned to 32KB total payload across items to balance latency and memory
Expose cloning helper that prefers downstream tee() for Web Streams when available; fall back to buffering+replay for AsyncIterator fanout
Do not implement 'perfect' resumable token-level delivery for now; instead support idempotent re-requests with best-effort partial offsets and a clear API to surface resume points to callers
Bundle surface will remain opt-in: new helpers live behind an import path "@redwood/sdk/streams-gateway" to avoid increasing default SDK size
tradeoffs: Pros of CancelController: predictable behavior across runtimes. Cons: another abstraction to maintain and teach developers
Buffer ring reduces OOM risk but may add copy overhead for some workloads; we tuned default watermarks conservatively
Resumable semantics simplified to avoid complex server-side state coupling; this limits zero-loss resume in adversarial failure modes
Fanout via tee() is cheap in browsers but not in AsyncIterator world; buffer-based fanout increases memory usage when many consumers are slow
risks: Edge-case regressions in older Node versions (12/14 compatibility) when polyfills are used
Subtle differences between WHATWG ReadableStream spec variants across runtimes could cause consumer-visible behavioral drift
Performance regressions if buffer strategy is misconfigured for high-throughput customers
Unclear mental model for customers if both toAsyncIterator() and toWebStream() are available without strong docs
comments: 2025-02-11: Kickoff meeting with SDK and runtime teams. Agreed to keep API minimal and opt-in.

2025-02-18: Prototype adapters working for Node 18 fetch ReadableStream -> AsyncIterator. Observed bursty memory when consumer sleeps for >500ms without backpressure enabled. Filed follow-up perf tasks.
2025-02-22: Design review with PM & DX. PM asked for example showing migration from older stream helpers; DX suggested smaller helper names to avoid friction in docs.
2025-02-25: Implemented CancelController and wired through fetch adapter. Initial tests show cancellation latency under 30ms on warm connections.
2025-02-28: PR opened: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/4875. Requesting review from @sophia-liu and @ryan-kell. Pending feedback on default watermark values.
2025-03-01: UX feedback: prefer 'toAsyncIterator' over 'asAsyncIterator' for naming consistency with other SDKs. Updating spec accordingly.
test_plan: Unit tests for adapter conversions (Node Readable <-> AsyncIterator, ReadableStream <-> AsyncIterator)
Simulated network flakiness integration test that cuts TCP after N bytes and validates graceful cancellation and resume points
Backpressure soak test: 1000 concurrent streams with slow consumers (100ms per chunk) to detect memory growth
Cross-runtime smoke: run examples in Node 18, Deno 1.35, Chrome 118, and Firefox on CI
API contract tests to assert that cancellation triggers underlying HTTP abort and that no additional data is emitted after cancel
rollout_plan: Merge behind feature flag 'streamsGateway' and ship to canary NPM tag
Gather telemetry for memory and cancellation latencies from opt-in customers for 2 weeks
Promote to latest tag if no regressions; publish migration guide and examples
Deprecate old helpers in 3 releases with clear codemod instructions
migration_notes: Existing consumers using older helpers will be able to keep using them. Recommend migrating to toAsyncIterator()/toWebStream() for new code and for cases where cancellation semantics matter. Provide a codemod and examples in the migration PR.
